problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.
problems.io:
Input
nums: int[]
1 ≤ n ≤ 105, -109 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 109
Output
boolean — true if duplicate exists
Example 1
nums = [1,2,3,1]
Output: true
// 1 appears at index 0 and 3
Example 2
nums = [1,2,3,4]
Output: false
problems.understanding: Brute force compares every pair — O(n²). Key insight: we only need to know "have I seen this before?" → Hash Set gives O(1) lookup, making one linear pass sufficient.

naive.title: Naive Solution — O(n²) Brute Force
naive.html:
Check every pair (i, j) with i < j. Return true on first match.

Expected Output
[1,2,3,1] → true  |  [1,2,3,4] → false

problems.intuition: "Have I seen this before?" → Hash Set. Store each number as we go; check the set before inserting. O(1) average lookup replaces O(n) inner scan.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize empty set seen.
  2. For each num: if num in seen → return True.
  3. Else add num to seen.
  4. End of loop → return False.

optimal.title: Optimized Code — Hash Set O(n)
optimal.html:
Expected Output
[1,2,3,1] → true  |  [1,2,3,4] → false  |  [1,1,1,3] → true

problems.variants:
Method 1 — Hash Set · O(n) / O(n) ✓ Recommended

Build a hash set on-the-fly. O(1) lookup with early exit.

Method 2 — Sorting · O(n log n) / O(1)

Sort in-place, check adjacent elements. Better space, worse time.

Method 3 — Python One-liner · O(n) / O(n)

return len(nums) != len(set(nums)) — No early exit though.
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Frequency Hashing — "Have I seen this before?" → Hash Set. This is the #1 most common array pattern, foundational to Two Sum, Group Anagrams, Longest Consecutive Sequence, and hundreds more problems.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.statement: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s. An anagram uses the exact same characters with identical frequencies.
problems.io:
Input
s, t: str (lowercase English letters)
1 ≤ len ≤ 5×104
Output
boolean — true if anagram
Example 1
s="anagram", t="nagaram"
Output: true
Example 2
s="rat", t="car"
Output: false
problems.constraints:
• 1 ≤ s.length, t.length ≤ 5×104
  • s and t consist of lowercase English letters
problems.understanding: Anagrams share identical character frequency distributions. Quick check: if lengths differ, immediately false. Then compare frequency maps — a hashmap/counter approach is O(n).

naive.title: Naive Solution — Sorting
naive.html:
Sort both strings. If anagrams, sorted versions are equal.

Expected Output
"anagram","nagaram" → true | "rat","car" → false

problems.intuition: Count character frequencies with a hashmap. Two strings are anagrams iff their frequency maps are identical. Single O(n) pass instead of O(n log n) sort.
problems.approach:
1. If len(s) != len(t) → return False.
  2. Build frequency map for s.
  3. For each char in t, decrement its count.
  4. If any count goes negative → return False.
  5. Return True.

optimal.title: Optimized Code — HashMap O(n)
optimal.html:
Expected Output
"anagram","nagaram" → true | "rat","car" → false

problems.variants:
Method 1 — Counter · O(n) / O(1) ✓

Counter(s) == Counter(t) — cleanest Python one-liner.

Method 2 — Fixed Array[26] · O(n) / O(1)

Integer array of size 26. Faster in practice due to cache locality.

Method 3 — Sorting · O(n log n) / O(1)

Sort both strings and compare. Simple but suboptimal.
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Character Frequency Map — "Same characters, different order" → compare frequency maps. Applies to anagram detection, permutation checking, group-by-signature problems.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one solution exists. You may not use the same element twice.
problems.io:
Input
nums: int[], target: int
2 ≤ n ≤ 104
Output
int[2] — indices [i, j] where nums[i]+nums[j]=target
Example 1
nums=[2,7,11,15], target=9
Output: [0,1]
// 2+7=9
Example 2
nums=[3,2,4], target=6
Output: [1,2]
problems.constraints:
• 2 ≤ nums.length ≤ 104
  • -109 ≤ nums[i], target ≤ 109
  • Only one valid answer exists
problems.understanding: For each element x, we need target - x. Brute force checks all pairs O(n²). Optimization: store each element in a map as we scan, look up the complement in O(1).

naive.title: Naive Solution — O(n²)
naive.html:
Check all pairs (i, j) with i < j.

Expected Output
[2,7,11,15],target=9 → [0,1]

problems.intuition: For each element x, we need target - x. Store visited elements in {value: index} map. Check if the complement exists before inserting current element.
problems.approach:
1. Init empty map seen = {value: index}.
  2. For each index i: compute complement = target - nums[i].
  3. If complement in seen → return [seen[complement], i].
  4. Else store seen[nums[i]] = i.

optimal.title: Optimized Code — One-pass HashMap
optimal.html:
Expected Output
[2,7,11,15],9 → [0,1] | [3,2,4],6 → [1,2] | [3,3],6 → [0,1]

problems.variants:
Method 1 — One-pass HashMap · O(n) / O(n) ✓

Check complement before inserting. Handles [3,3] edge case correctly.

Method 2 — Two-pass HashMap · O(n) / O(n)

Build full map, then scan for complement. Slightly simpler, same complexity.

Method 3 — Two Pointers (if sorted) · O(n log n) / O(1)

Sort + two pointers. O(1) space but loses original indices.
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Complement Lookup via HashMap — Store visited elements, check complement on each step. Canonical HashMap-in-arrays pattern. Generalizes to 3Sum (sort + fix + two-ptr) and 4Sum.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.statement: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. Return in any order.
problems.understanding: Anagrams share the same character frequency signature. Use sorted string as the hashmap key to group all anagrams together.
problems.intuition: "eat" sorted = "aet", "tea" sorted = "aet", "ate" sorted = "aet". Use this canonical form as a dict key to group them in one pass.
problems.approach:
1. Init groups = defaultdict(list).
  2. For each string s, compute key = tuple(sorted(s)).
  3. Append s to groups[key].
  4. Return list(groups.values()).
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Group by Canonical Form — When grouping equivalent items, normalize to a canonical signature and use it as a hashmap key.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements.
problems.constraints:
• 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 105
  • k is in range [1, number of unique elements]
  • The answer is guaranteed to be unique
problems.intuition: Bucket Sort: Frequencies range 1 to n. Create n+1 frequency buckets. Put numbers into their bucket. Read from the end (highest freq) until we have k elements. O(n) — beats heap's O(n log k).
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Bucket Sort for Bounded Frequencies — When frequency values are bounded by n, bucket sort achieves O(n). "Top K" problems: use heap O(n log k) or bucket sort O(n).

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.statement: Return array where answer[i] = product of all elements except nums[i]. Must run O(n) without division.
problems.intuition: answer[i] = product_of_all_left × product_of_all_right. Two passes: left to right (prefix), right to left (suffix). Combine into result in O(n) with O(1) extra space.
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Prefix/Suffix Accumulation — "Everything to the left × everything to the right." Applies to Trapping Rain Water, Max Product Subarray. Avoids division.

problems.title: Valid Sudoku
problems.statement: Determine if a 9×9 Sudoku board is valid. Each row, column, and 3×3 sub-box must contain digits 1–9 without repetition. Empty cells are '.'.
problems.intuition: Track seen digits per row, column, and box simultaneously in ONE pass. Box index: (r//3)*3 + (c//3). If any digit repeats in any set → invalid.
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Multi-Constraint Tracking in One Pass — Maintain separate sets for each constraint dimension. Box formula: (r//3)*3 + c//3.

problems.title: Encode and Decode Strings
problems.statement: Design encode/decode for a list of strings to a single string. Must handle any characters including #, |, etc.
problems.intuition: Length-prefix encoding: Format each string as "{length}#{content}". During decode, read the length, skip #, read exactly that many chars. No delimiter collisions possible.
problems.takeaway: Pattern: Length-Prefix Encoding — Encode variable-length data with a length prefix to avoid delimiter ambiguity. Used in HTTP/2 framing, protobuf, network protocols.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.statement: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the length of the longest consecutive sequence. Must run in O(n) time.
problems.io:
Example 1
nums = [100,4,200,1,3,2]
Output: 4
// Sequence: 1,2,3,4
Example 2
nums = [0,3,7,2,5,8,4,6,0,1]
Output: 9
problems.understanding: A number is a sequence start only if n-1 is NOT in the set. Only count from starts to avoid O(n²). Total while-loop iterations across all starts = n (amortized O(n)).
problems.intuition: Convert to set for O(1) lookup. For each number, only start counting if it has no predecessor (n-1 not in set). Then count upward. Each element processed at most twice total.
problems.approach:
1. Put all numbers in a hash set.
  2. For each n: if n-1 not in set (sequence start):
  3.     Count up: while n+len in set, increment length.
  4.     Update best = max(best, length).
  5. Return best.

optimal.title: Optimized Code — Hash Set O(n)
optimal.html: Pattern: Hash Set for Sequence Detection — Convert to set for O(1) lookup. Start counting only from "sequence beginners" (n-1 not in set). Amortized O(n) because total iterations across all sequences = n.
